solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Follow on to make certain when down on runs

indicators.note: to be down on something is to be short of it, so a letter is missing

blocks.note: to ensure is to make certain
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A cricket instruction: enforce the follow-on once the other side is well short on runs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follow on' is cricket jargon in the surface, but here it just means come after. Take the R out of ENSURE to leave ENSUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to happen afterwards as a consequence, which is what following on means in ordinary speech.

clue.text: Record is old recording son’s put out as not playing continuously

indicators.note: something put out has been ejected, so a letter is thrown out of the word

blocks.note: an EP is an extended-play record
O is the standard abbreviation for old
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A record collector grumbles that an old disc skips and will not play straight through.
explanation.walkthrough: An EP (extended play) was a short vinyl record with a few tracks; the son is dropped from the second recording word only.
explanation.definitionFit: Something episodic happens in separate instalments or bursts rather than running continuously without a break.

clue.text: Cast mostly delivered almost any playwright

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
almost means just short of the whole, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: to shed is to cast off, as a snake casts its skin
rid in the old sense of delivered or freed

explanation.surface: A theatre producer claims that nearly any dramatist could be cast in a delivered play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' pretends to be about actors but means shed. Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote The School for Scandal and The Rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan was an eighteenth-century Irish dramatist, famous for comedies of manners staged in London theatres.

clue.text: Displaced ancient freshmen no longer being denied a vote

definitions.text: no longer being denied a vote

indicators.note: things displaced are moved out of their places, so the letters shift into a new order

explanation.surface: Elderly first-year students, pushed out of their homes, finally win the right to vote.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words together supply exactly the fifteen letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Enfranchisement is the granting of voting rights, the condition of people who are no longer excluded from the ballot.

clue.text: Novel and difficult crossword you’ve got here?

blocks.note: this puzzle is the Times crossword, so the one in front of you is the Times

explanation.surface: The setter teases the solver: is this a tricky puzzle in front of you?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue points at itself: you are solving a Times puzzle. 'Novel' reads as new but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard Times is a Charles Dickens book of 1854, set in the industrial town of Coketown.

clue.text: Tramp having ferret round

blocks.note: a hob is a male ferret

explanation.surface: A vagrant keeps a pet ferret with him on his travels.
explanation.walkthrough: HOB for a male ferret is crossword stock, as is O for anything round.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobo is an American word for a homeless wanderer, the same figure a British speaker calls a tramp.

clue.text: Choral rite reworked aiming at maximum vocal effect

indicators.note: something reworked has been redone in a different form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A church service for choir is rearranged so the singing makes the biggest impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vocal' fits the choir in the surface but belongs to the definition, which is about speech designed to impress.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhetorical language is crafted for persuasive or showy effect on listeners rather than for plain information.

clue.text: One’s left Euston, say, without proposal for the moving of stock?

indicators.note: whatever has left is gone, so that letter is taken away
without in its old sense of outside, so these letters go round another word

blocks.note: Euston is a London railway terminus

explanation.surface: A traveller leaves Euston station with no plan, perhaps about moving shares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' suggests shares but means plants, as in nursery stock. Euston is a mainline station in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Transplantation is the moving of growing plants from one bed to another, and garden plants are called stock.

clue.text: Silver grabbed by politician that is an obsessive collector

indicators.note: what is grabbed ends up held inside the grabber's grip

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
MP is a Member of Parliament
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A greedy politician pockets the silver, the kind of hoarder who grabs everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' is not a link phrase here: it supplies the abbreviation i.e. at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Magpies are reputed to steal shiny objects, so a person who hoards things compulsively is called one.

clue.text: Arab chief needs the man captured by a believer

indicators.note: a captive is held inside, so one word goes within another

blocks.note: a Sikh is a follower of the Sikh faith

explanation.surface: A desert leader needs his man, who has been taken prisoner by a religious zealot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A believer' is vague on purpose; it is a member of one particular faith whose four-letter name holds the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheikh is the leader of an Arab family, tribe or village, so a chief among Arabs.

clue.text: Awfully fine story never to be told

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the letters come out in a mangled order

explanation.surface: A tale so wonderful it must be kept secret for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully fine' reads as a gushing phrase, but 'Awfully' works on FINE and the story's word together.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineffable means too great or sacred to be expressed in words, so it can never be spoken or described.

clue.text: Get upset, dismissing judge’s viewpoint

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: nerves that jangle are jarred and upset
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper when a judge throws out their point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the J from JANGLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An angle is a particular slant or perspective on a subject, much the same thing as a standpoint.

clue.text: One seen in seedy city area, topless and with an American

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter is cut off
to be seen in a place is to be inside it

blocks.note: Soho is a district of central London long known for sleaze
an taken as written, with meaning added

explanation.surface: A topless visitor spotted in a sleazy part of town, accompanied by an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests a nightclub act but only beheads the district, a London area once famous for strip clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ohioan is a native of Ohio, a US state, so the answer names a particular kind of American.

clue.text: What’s useful when flying parasite puts an end to pleasures

indicators.note: putting an end to something means attaching a piece at its finish

blocks.note: a tick is a blood-sucking parasite

explanation.surface: A flying insect ruins the fun, as bugs on a picnic do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts an end to' reads as spoils but means sits at the end of. 'Flying parasite' seems a unit, yet 'flying' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A joystick is the control lever a pilot uses to steer an aircraft, so it is needed in the air.

clue.text: Like some birds, perch above feline climbing in conifer

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means going upward, so the letters run backward
in places these letters inside another word
in a down clue above means placed before the next piece

explanation.surface: A bird perches over a cat that is climbing a pine tree after it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'above' just means comes first; the tree's name is split after its first letter to take both pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Psittacine means relating to parrots, so it describes one family of birds such as parakeets and macaws.

clue.text: Impossible to visit current vandalised science labs

indicators.note: vandalised things are smashed up, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

blocks.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: School labs have been trashed and are closed to visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' wants to be AC, but only I makes the letter count work with the labs.
explanation.definitionFit: A place that is inaccessible cannot be reached or entered, so nobody is able to go there.

clue.text: One returning home to sound off about flat

indicators.note: about means around, so one word surrounds another

blocks.note: to sound off is to rant

explanation.surface: Someone comes back home and complains loudly about the apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like a home but means level. The definition is fair because a ghost is one who comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: A revenant is a ghost or person who returns, especially from the dead, to haunt a former home.

clue.text: Concerned with area in European Article 50 that’s delicate

indicators.note: in puts these letters inside the others

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A question about some part of the EU treaty clause on leaving, a sensitive matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Article 50 is the EU treaty clause used for Brexit, but here it is split: THE plus L.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal means extremely light and fine, almost too airy for this world, so delicate in substance.

clue.text: Educate employees in district in the seizure of debtors’ goods

indicators.note: to be in a place is to be enclosed by it

blocks.note: DIST is the abbreviation for district

explanation.surface: Local staff are trained in how to repossess goods from people who owe money.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is the container signal; the second joins wordplay to definition. Employees as 'men' is an old crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Distrainment, or distraint, is the legal process of taking someone's property to settle unpaid money they owe.

clue.text: Take fruit and small cakes, giving the last three away

indicators.note: giving something away means losing it, here the final three letters

explanation.surface: A tea-time scene of taking fruit and little cakes, though handing the last few to someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: A crumpet is a British spongy griddle cake eaten toasted. Scrump is a British word used of children raiding orchards.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrump is to steal apples or other produce from an orchard, a British term for petty pilfering.

clue.text: Corpse’s being interred shortly, but court case’s not begun

indicators.note: cut short means the final letter is dropped
not begun means the first letter is missing

blocks.note: a court case is a trial

explanation.surface: A body is to be buried soon, although the court hearing has not yet started.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' seems to mean soon but actually cuts the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A burial is the act of putting a dead body in the ground, which is what interring a corpse means.

clue.text: Prompt passage crossing to island

blocks.note: a passage is a way through

explanation.surface: A quick ferry trip over to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prompt' looks like an adjective for punctual but is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A causeway is a raised road across water or marsh, often linking the mainland with an offshore island.

clue.text: After what may be draughts, vacated the cell

indicators.note: a vacated space has been emptied, so only the outer letters remain
after means following, so one piece comes behind the other

blocks.note: draughts is an example of a game

explanation.surface: A prisoner, after cold draughts, finally moves out of the chilly cell.
explanation.walkthrough: Draughts is the British name for checkers. 'Cell' suggests a prison but is biological.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamete is a reproductive cell, such as a sperm or egg, which fuses with another at fertilisation.

clue.text: Bowl over duration of test match, it’s reported

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by the sound

blocks.note: a Test match in cricket lasts up to five days

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator reports a bowler's efforts over the length of a Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl over' sounds like cricket but means stun. A Test match is an international cricket game lasting up to five days.
explanation.definitionFit: To bowl someone over is to astonish or stun them, leaving them dazed and bewildered.

clue.text: Join train in the middle to return

indicators.note: the middle means the centre, so only the inner letters are kept
to return is to go back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a retinue is a train of attendants; its inner five letters

explanation.surface: A passenger boards a train halfway along the line for the journey back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' wants to be a railway train or to teach, but here it is RETINUE, a train of followers.
explanation.definitionFit: To unite is to bring together or combine into one, which is what joining things does.

clue.text: Being silly about one carpet that’s beyond livening up

indicators.note: about means around, so one set of letters goes round the other

blocks.note: a mat is a small carpet

explanation.surface: Someone fusses daftly over a rug too drab ever to be brightened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Livening up' hints at brightening a room, but the definition means incapable of being brought to life.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inanimate has no life in it at all, so it cannot be brought to life or animated.

clue.text: Openly upset about article offering invented material

indicators.note: upset things are knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged
about means around, so these letters wrap the next piece

explanation.surface: Someone is visibly distressed about a newspaper piece containing fabricated content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invented material' suggests made-up copy, but it is a synthetic substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Polythene is a man-made plastic, a synthetic material devised in a laboratory rather than found in nature.

clue.text: Referring to very early start, the French bronze has to be returned

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a bronze skin colour is a tan

explanation.surface: An early-morning trip: the French sunbather must hand back the bronze medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bronze' suggests a medal but is a suntan.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal describes things relating to birth, the very first beginning of a person's life.
